images.caption: Figure 1:Asynchronous reasoning with agent-directed coordination.Left: Schematic timelines show parallel preparation with ordered vase access, and lead takeover followed by delegated finishing for towel folding. Top right: Mean physical progress and time cost across six tasks, with five trials per policy. Bottom right: Task-level time comparisons between Direct and ACAP in the task-coverage and repeated-trial studies.

Figure 2:Independent policy loops with agentic coordination.(a) Member agents serve configurable control groups, illustrated by two arms with grippers and a body group comprising the torso and chassis. (b) The hyper-agent policyπH\pi_{H}uses historyhkh_{k}and member reports to assign or revise work, authorize access, or arrange direct lead execution of coupled actions. Each member follows an independent observe–reason–code–execute loop. The ownership checkωk​(c)\omega_{k}(c)permits only the current owner to command groupcc. (c) Persistent contexts, message buffers, event-based waits and exclusive ownership support asynchronous progress and coordinated control handoffs.

Figure 3:Visible progress with Direct and ACAP.Three cases cover Fully Parallel and Parallel-Sequential tasks across Galaxea R1 Pro and two AgileX PiPER installations. Columns share elapsed times within each task. Row labels give observed episode durations, andendedmarks repeated final images.

Figure 4:Coordination on Collaborative tasks.ACAP uses direct lead execution for towel folding and complementary member roles for bottle opening. Columns share elapsed times.Faileddenotes task noncompletion. Both bottle baselines trigger hardware faults after arm crossing. Later Fixed columns repeat its last available image.

images.caption: Figure 8:Geometric reasoning for action and feedback.(a) The robot raises the flower. The agent uses the measured hand displacement and two images to estimate the tip’s position, then aligns and inserts the stem. (b) The agent estimates basket placement and clearance from fitted surfaces and tracked motion, then adjusts both arms to lower and release the basket. (c) A fitted bottle axis determines a corrective wrist rotation, which is used in the next motion command before tray placement. (d) After a commanded 20 mm lift, tracked carton features indicate a rise of approximately 19 mm, correcting the lead’s initial slip diagnosis.
Figure 9:Fully Parallel tasks.Direct andACAPperform battery placement, wiping and towel arrangement, towel-roll placement, and independent cube/battery sorting.
Figure 10:Parallel-Sequential tasks.Direct andACAPperform pen placement on two installations, grid sorting, flower insertion and clothes collection.

Figure 11:Parallel-Sequential tasks (continued).Sponge-cube placement, cup stacking, toy-block collection, four-flower insertion and towel-pyramid construction. The towel-pyramid sequence has its own column times.
Figure 12:Collaborative tasks.Direct, Fixed andACAPperform basket lifting on R1, shirt folding on P-C and fruit-basket lifting on P-A.

Figure 13:Collaborative tasks (continued).Milk-carton lifting, pot placement on a book and fruit-basket placement on a sponge. Direct andACAPachieve task completion in all three settings. Fixed leaves the pot and basket tasks unfinished in these runs.
